added: == Video ==
{{Video:Take Care of Young Children|}}

#Have a snack ready for the children when they wake up. It doesn't need to be elaborate, but at least make it healthy. You can have graham crackers and milk, low fat yogurt, pretzel sticks and cheese, or apple slices and grapes; on occasions, you can offer a treat if it's a special day (e.g. a birthday).<ref>[v161407_b01]. 13 April 2020.</ref>[[Image:Take Care of Young Children Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Establish a before-bed routine that everyone can easily adjust to.<ref>[v161407_b01]. 13 April 2020.</ref> You might need to give them a bath, have them brush and floss their teeth, and brush their hair before tucking them in. If the children need a bath, see if each one wants to bathe individually or together in the same tub. Keep the water up to their waists to prevent drowning, and test the water by dipping your elbow in the water to see if it's too hot or too cold. You elbow is more sensitive than your fingertips.[[Image:Take Care of Young Children Step 11.jpg|center]]

#Read the children a bedtime story or sing songs before they sleep.<ref>[v161407_b01]. 13 April 2020.</ref> Have each child pick out one book that you can read to them, or one song each you can sing to avoid fighting and disagreement. Then, once you're finished with that, you can tuck them in and tell them good night before turning off any lights and leaving the room. You can crack the door if you want to be able to hear them talking or moving around. Some children may want a night light in their room if they have a fear of the dark.[[Image:Take Care of Young Children Step 12.jpg|center]]

You can have an alarm go off for the children to wake up to, such as a favorite children's song or a soft bell. Avoid something too loud, such as a rooster crowing or rock music. If they don't wake up right away, you can gently tap them and say something such as, "Hey, it's time to get up, sleepyhead". Once they are awake, you can start getting them ready for the day by getting them dressed, doing their hair, and brushing their teeth.[[Image:Take Care of Young Children Step 1.jpg|center]]

added: Young children, ranging from toddlers to those who have just started school, are all different in their own way. That's why you as a parent, guardian, relative, or babysitter play a crucial part in their development. Not only are you helping their fine, gross, and motor skills develop, you're shaping their perspective of life and their surroundings each and every time you are with them. Taking care of a young child might seem challenging at first, especially with all of the tantrums and crying, but by the end of the day you'll be a pro. Read on to discover how you can take care of young children!

#* Make music with pots and pans
#* Do finger-painting

#* Take them to your local library, if they offer a storytime for younger children
#* Order fun science or history kits that are suitable for small children
#* Take nature walks and explain something to them, such as the metamorphosis of a butterfly if you see a caterpillar.

While they nap, you can either sit in the room and nap with them or accomplish a few things as long as you keep quiet. Though you might want to make a phone call or do your nails, that can most likely wait until later.

# Time to play again! Take advantage of the warm weather if possible and visit your local playground, kick a soccer ball in the backyard, blow bubbles, draw with chalk, chase butterflies, or run through the sprinklers. Cut off all screen time an hour before bed by giving a warning such as, "Okay girls, you have ten more minutes to finish watching Paw Patrol before the TV goes off."

# Establish a before-bed routine that everyone can easily adjust to. You might need to give them a bath, have them brush and floss their teeth, and brush their hair before tucking them in. If the children need a bath, see if each one wants to bathe individually or together in the same tub. Keep the water up to their waists to prevent drowning, and test the water by dipping your elbow in the water to see if it's too hot or too cold. You elbow is more sensitive than your fingertips.

# Read the children a bedtime story or sing songs before they sleep. Have each child pick out one book that you can read to them, or one song each you can sing to avoid fighting and disagreement. Then, once you're finished with that, you can tuck them in and tell them good night before turning off any lights and leaving the room. You can crack the door if you want to be able to hear them talking or moving around. Some children may want a night light in their room if they have a fear of the dark.

* Allow the kids to help you clean around the house, such as picking up their toys and putting them away. This teaches them responsibility and gives them the knowledge they need to know that they should do this task when required.
* To help a child learn how to say something, repeat the word slowly and break it down for them, until they can say it clearly or to where you can understand them.

You can have a dance party, build a blanket fort and watch a movie or read under it, bake cookies (always supervise the children if you want to use the oven or stove), or play children's board games (i.e. Candyland, Operation, etc.).

# Soon you'll need to feed the kids dinner. Spaghetti and meatballs, a taco or salad bar, grilled cheese and tomato soup, or a vegetable dish are all great options. You can have a theme night, such as rainbow dinner or Italian night. Why not go out to eat or order pizza even? If you're babysitting, be sure to ask the parents for money to pay for takeout/pizza; if you end up using your money, politely ask that they reimburse you.

# There should be a space of an hour or two (or even three) before you get the kids ready for bed. Don't do anything too strenuous to get them hyper before bed; you can mold with Play Dough or watch a kid-friendly movie. Cut off all screen time an hour before bed by giving a warning such as, "Okay girls, you have ten more minutes to finish watching Paw Patrol before the TV goes off."

Keep the water up to their waists to prevent drowning, and test the water by dipping your elbow in the water to see if it's too hot or too cold. You elbow is more sensitive then your fingertips.

added: Young children, ranging from toddlers to those who have just started school, are all different in their own way. That's why you as a parent, guardian, relative, or babysitter play a crucial part in their development. Not only are you helping their fine, gross, and motor skills develop, you're shaping their perspective of life and their surroundings each and every time you are with them. Taking care of a young child might seem challenging at first, especially with all of the tantrums and crying, but by the end of the day you'll be a pro. Read on to discover how you can take care of young children!
== Steps ==

# Have a set time for the children to wake up. This can easily be adjusted when necessary, but start with a time such as seven thirty or eight in the morning. Once they are awake, you can start getting them ready for the day by getting them dressed, doing their hair, and brushing their teeth (if they're a bit older, they should know how to brush their teeth unless they need help still or are physically unable to).

#* You can have an alarm go off for the children to wake up to, such as a favorite children's song or a soft bell. Avoid something too loud, such as a rooster crowing or rock music. If they don't wake up right away, you can gently tap them and say something such as, "Hey, it's time to get up, sleepyhead."

# Make sure you feed them a healthy, nutrition-filled breakfast. Breakfast is the most important meal of the day, enabling a child to have strength to last them throughout the day. Allow them to help you with a simple task they can accomplish; allowing them to hold the cups while you pour the milk or assemble their own yogurt parfait are both great ways to get them involved! The following are good breakfast ideas you and the young children can enjoy:

#* Yogurt Parfaits: All you need for this is vanilla or plain yogurt, blueberries, cut-up strawberries, and granola. Let each child make their own parfait, even if they add a little too much granola on top.

#* Special Toast: Of course, you can pop some bread into the toaster, spread jam or peanut butter on it, and serve the kids that. But who wants to be boring? Once the bread's toasted and you've got your spread on it, get everyone involved by making faces on it! Use apple slices for the mouth, grapes for eyes, and blueberries for the mouth.

#* Eggs and Bacon: You can easily crack several eggs in a bowl, mix them together, and cook them to make a large batch of scrambled eggs for breakfast. Bacon's easy to cook as well; just follow the directions on the package.

#* Cereal: Ah, every kid's favorite. Avoid cereals with a high content of sugar, unless you want the kids bouncing on the walls! If the kids have any dairy allergies or are lactose intolerant, substitute normal milk for milk made out of almonds, cashews, soy, or coconuts.

# Now, it's time to play! Vary each activity you do, since young children tend to get bored very easily. Why not pretend to be pirates trying to find treasure in the living room, play dress up with costumes and other silly accessories, read stories, build a race track for cars or marbles, make music with pots and pans, do finger-painting, or create a game of your own that just requires imagination and whatever props you need? Don't get mad if things stray a little off course; remember to just roll with it and have fun!

#* Want to encourage learning without the children knowing? Incorporate it wherever possible! Take them to your local library if they offer a storytime for younger children weekly, order fun science or history kits that are suitable for small children, or take nature walks and explain something to them, such as the metamorphosis of a butterfly if you see a caterpillar. Try the website ABCmouse.com, which provides learning opportunities that are fun and engaging for ages 2-8.

# Around 11 a.m. to noon, you should serve lunch. Again, allow the kids to help out whenever possible. You can make ham and cheese sandwiches (cut the bread with a cookie cutter to make the bread look cool), mac n' cheese, chicken nuggets, or crackers with luncheon meat and cheese. Add healthy sides, such as a cheese stick, carrot sticks with ranch dressing, strawberries, or applesauce.

# Once lunch is over, the children will need a nap. Set them on their beds or on the couch with a pillow, a blanket, and their favorite stuffed animal; turn on calming music on your phone or white noise; and limit your noises as the children sleep. While they nap, you can either sit in the room and nap with them or accomplish a few things as long as you keep quiet. Though you might want to make a phone call or do your nails, that can most likely wait until later.

# Have a snack ready for the children when they wake up. It doesn't need to be elaborate, but at least make it healthy. You can have graham crackers and milk, pretzel sticks and cheese, or apple slices and grapes; on occassion, you can offer a treat if it's a special day (i.e. a birthday).

# Time to play again! Take advantage of the warm weather if possible and visit your local playground, kick a soccer ball in the backyard, blow bubbles, draw with chalk, chase butterflies, or run through the sprinklers. Too stormy or cold? You can have a dance party, build a blanket fort and watch a movie or read under it, bake cookies (always supervise the children if you want to use the oven or stove), or play children's board games (i.e. Candyland, Operation, etc.).

# Soon you'll need to feed the kids dinner. Spaghetti and meatballs, a taco or salad bar, grilled cheese and tomato soup, or a vegetable dish are all great options. You can have a theme night, such as rainbow dinner or Italian night. Why not go out to eat or order pizza even? If you're babysitting, be sure to ask the parents for money to pay for takeout/pizza; if you end up using your money, politely ask that they reimburse you.

# There should be a space of an hour or two (or even three) before you get the kids ready for bed. Don't do anything too strenuous to get them hyper before bed; you can mold with Play Dough or watch a kid-friendly movie. Cut off all screen time an hour before bed by giving a warning such as, "Okay girls, you have ten more minutes to finish watching Paw Patrol before the TV goes off."

# Establish a before bed routine that everyone can easily adjust to. You might need to give them a bath, have them brush and floss their teeth, and brush their hair before tucking them in. If the children need a bath, see if each one wants to bathe individually or together in the same tub. Keep the water up to their waists to prevent drowning, and test the water by dipping your elbow in the water to see if it's too hot or too cold. You elbow is more sensitive then your fingertips.

# As an option, the children might want you to read them a bedtime story or sing them songs before they sleep. Have each child pick out one book that you can read to them or one song each you can sing to avoid fighting and disagreement. Then, once you're finished with that, you can tuck them in and tell them good night before turning off any lights and leaving the room. You can crack the door in case you hear them talking or moving around, and they may want a night light in their room if they have a fear of the dark.
== Tips ==

* Allow the kids to help you clean around the house, even if it's something such as picking up their toys and putting them away. This teaches them responsibility and gives them the knowledge they need to know that they should do this task when required.

* Because young children are still learning to communicate, they might not be able to fully tell you if they're hungry or thirsty. Ask them on a regular basis if they need a snack or need water to drink, and always ask whenever necessary if they need to use the restroom.
* If you're babysitting and the parents have given you the money to order pizza or another kind of food, be sure that you hold on to all receipts for proof.
* To help a child learn how to say something, repeat the word slowly and break it down for them until they can say it clearly or to where you can understand them.

* If you see a child clutching their pants or squirming, these are tell tale signs that they need to use the restroom. Quickly escort them to the bathroom, and don't make a big deal if they have an accident. Just keep your cool as you tell them, "It's okay! There's always next time!" before helping them.
* Limit their screen time from thirty minutes to an hour and a half. They don't need to be spending a lot of time playing games or watching movies!
== Warnings ==

* Keep all cleaning products, medications or vitamins, matches, knives, lighters, cigarettes, and sharp appliances away from the children's reach. You may want to lock cabinets that the children can reach that contain any of these things.

* If the children are old enough, be sure that you teach them their address, their full name, and their parents' or guardians' names. If one of them was lost, they can easily recite this if they find someone to help them.
